echoes.note: Paul's rhetorical 'the saints will judge the world' draws directly on the eschatological assize of Dan 7:22, where judgment is given to 'the saints of the Most High' who then possess the kingdom. Volume is high (the distinctive pairing of holy ones + judgment + world dominion), and the theme coheres with Paul's argument that believers should not need pagan courts now since they will judge the cosmos. Availability is secure as a canonical apocalyptic source.

'They will judge nations and rule over peoples' provides a close Second-Temple parallel to the saints judging the world (v.2), framing the righteous as future judges/rulers in the age to come. Recurrence of this motif across Daniel, Wisdom, and 1 Enoch strengthens its availability, though Paul's wording is closer to Daniel; Wisdom supplies the wider tradition.

The saints (hasidim) executing the written judgment upon the nations supplies a faint coherent backdrop to believers judging the world. Volume is low and verbal links are absent, but the motif of the holy ones as agents of eschatological judgment recurs in the same stream Paul taps.

The pseudepigraphal tradition of the holy ones gathered to enact judgment, and of judgment falling even upon angelic Watchers (1 En 10-16), undergirds Paul's startling claim that 'we will judge angels' (v.3). Cited only because the angel-judgment motif is otherwise unattested in the canonical OT and Availability rests on this Second-Temple stream.

'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD' coheres tightly with Paul's 'Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?' (v.7), counseling the renunciation of self-vindication. The wisdom ethic of leaving redress to God, paired with the righteous-sufferer posture, gives medium volume coherence.

'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me' parallels Paul's preference to suffer wrong rather than retaliate through litigation. A faint, coherent wisdom echo within the same proverbial cluster as 20:22.

The vice list's prohibition of men lying with men (arsenokoitai, v.9) is widely understood to be coined from the LXX of Lev 18:22 (meta arsenos ou koimethese koiten gynaikos). High volume via the rare compound term and strong coherence with the Holiness Code's catalog of exclusionary sins.

Lev 20:13 repeats the same LXX phrase (arsenos koiten gynaikos) and adds the death penalty, reinforcing the lexical derivation of arsenokoitai and the kingdom-exclusion logic. Recurrence across both Holiness-Code chapters strengthens the allusion.

The prohibition of the cult prostitute (qadesh/qedeshah) and the refusal of the 'wage of a dog' coheres with Paul's pairing of malakoi/pornoi and idolaters in a vice list, since cultic prostitution joined sexual sin to idolatry. Medium volume; thematic rather than verbal.

The inclusion of adulterers (moichoi) and thieves in the catalog echoes the Decalogue's prohibitions of adultery and theft, the foundational covenant ethic underlying Paul's roster of those excluded from the kingdom. Coherent but diffuse, as vice lists conventionally absorb Decalogue categories.

'You were washed' (v.11) resonates with Ezekiel's new-covenant promise, 'I will sprinkle clean water on you and you shall be clean,' joined there to sanctification and the gift of the Spirit, exactly the triad Paul deploys (washed, sanctified, justified, in the Spirit). Coherence is strong; the cleansing-plus-Spirit pairing supports the allusion.

'Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove the evil of your deeds' offers a prophetic moral-cleansing backdrop to 'you were washed' following a vice list. Faint and contested against the stronger ritual/Spirit cleansing of Ezek 36:25.

'God raised up the Lord and will also raise us up by his power' (v.14) draws on the canonical hope of bodily resurrection first explicit in Dan 12:2 ('many who sleep in the dust shall awake'). Coherent with Paul's bodily theology against the slogan that the belly/body is destined for nothing; medium volume as the foundational OT resurrection text.

The martyrs' confidence of being raised up by God supplies a Second-Temple parallel to Paul's resurrection assurance in v.14, attesting the availability of bodily-resurrection hope. Faint and supplementary to Dan 12:2.

Paul explicitly cites Gen 2:24 with a citation formula ('For, he says, the two will become one flesh', v.16) to prove that union with a prostitute makes one body with her. High volume and an unambiguous LXX quotation; the creation text is wrenched into an argument it never anticipated, a paradigmatic Pauline use.

'He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit' (v.17) plays on the LXX language of cleaving/being joined (kollao) to the LORD found in Deut 10:20 ('him shall you cleave to'), the covenantal counter-image to illicit bodily union. Coherence is strong given the deliberate contrast Paul builds between the two kinds of joining.

Cleaving to the LORD as the source of life (LXX kollasthai) recurs here, reinforcing the covenantal 'joined to the Lord' motif of v.17. A faint recurrence within the Deuteronomic cleaving stream rather than a discrete source.

'Flee sexual immorality!' (v.18) evokes the paradigm of Joseph who literally fled and left his garment to escape Potiphar's wife, the canonical exemplar of fleeing porneia. Coherent and recognized in Jewish moral tradition (cf. Wisdom-Joseph paraenesis); medium volume by motif.

'Keep your way far from her, do not go near the door of her house' supplies the wisdom counsel to flee the adulteress lying behind Paul's imperative to flee porneia. Faint verbal contact but coherent within the same paraenetic tradition.

'Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit' (v.19) figurally transfers the sanctuary motif, 'let them make me a sanctuary that I may dwell among them,' onto the believer's body as God's indwelt dwelling. The Spirit-indwelling makes the body holy space; medium volume as a figural reapplication of tabernacle theology.

'I will make my dwelling among you... and walk among you' undergirds the temple-of-the-Spirit image, the covenant promise of God's indwelling presence now located in the believer's body. A coherent but diffuse echo supplementing the Exodus sanctuary text.
'My dwelling place shall be with them' continues the indwelling-sanctuary stream Paul figurally applies to the Spirit-filled body in v.19. Faint and recurrent rather than a single discrete source.

'You were bought with a price' (v.20) evokes the redemption language of Isa 52:3 ('you were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money'), reframing the believer as God's purchased possession who is no longer his own. Coherent with the surrounding new-exodus redemption motif; medium volume by theme.

The jubilee redemption-price legislation, where a person is bought back according to a reckoned price, supplies the legal-economic backdrop for 'bought with a price' and belonging now to another master. Faint and contested against the prophetic redemption of Isa 52:3.

'Whom I created for my glory' provides a faint backdrop to 'glorify God in your body' (v.20), the redeemed belonging to God for his glory. Low volume; offered as a possible coherent echo of the purpose-of-redemption theme.
